caught_by: team-lead reading /tmp/codex-verify-d2RuXV/ directly and finding only 2 of 12 stage logs present with no running process, rather than trusting the still-armed monitor's silence as evidence of progress
gap: the wait condition only tested for the exit-code file's existence, never for the wrapped process's own liveness -- so 'file absent' was read as 'still running' when it could equally mean 'process died before writing anything'
gate: operator/team-lead manual log inspection (no automated gate existed for this failure mode)
generalization: Five distinct instances in one day, three different agents, all the same shape -- treating a wrapper's state as evidence about the wrapped process's state, rather than checking the process itself: (1) a monitor armed on $! captured a wrapper PID, not cargo's child, and reported 'exited' while the real build ran 40 more minutes; (2) a poller watched log CONTENT, which stops changing when a run finishes, indistinguishable from a slow run; (3) a launcher timed out on a healthy vite dev server because startup logging looked idle; (4) a launcher timed out on a cold ~496-crate compile for the same reason; (5) this one -- a file-existence wait that could not tell 'still building' from 'died before writing anything'. This is the operational twin of decisions.md's Decision 36 (SD28-E16): a proxy standing in for a real source, diverging silently because nothing checks the two against each other. The fix pattern is the same in both domains -- check the real source directly (pgrep the actual process, not the wrapper's exit code; read the RESULT: line or exit-code file, not a log-pattern grep) rather than trusting a proxy's silence as a positive signal.
summary: verify.sh wait-monitor could not distinguish a live long build from a dead one -- generalized as the fifth instance today of a wrapper's own state being read as evidence about the process it wraps
would_have: an until-loop Monitor (`until [ -f exit_code ]; do sleep 30; done`) waiting forever on a verify.sh run that died mid-build without ever writing its exit-code file -- silently indistinguishable from a healthy multi-hour run, discovered only because team-lead noticed the wait had gone unusually long and checked the log directory directly
would_have_reached: branch (the cycle would have stalled indefinitely on this wait, never reaching a commit, until manually noticed)
